newsitem.title: CANADA: Potential bidders eyeing Morrison Pete -CEO.
newsitem.headline: Potential bidders eyeing Morrison Pete -CEO.

text.p: Takeover target Morrison Petroleums Ltd has received "serious" expressions of interest from potential rivals to predator Canadian 88 Energy Corp, Morrison chairman and chief executive Gordon Stollery said on Wednesday.

"There is serious interest from quite respectable companies that have plenty of talent to take over these exploration projects which we're doing -- both financial and technical talent," Stollery said in an interview after the company's release of 1996 financial results.
"There's also the possibility of Morrison to exist exactly as it is now. But that remains to be seen whether we can talk our shareholders into a longer-term strategy," he said.
Canadian 88 last week offered C$10 per share, up to a miximum of C$140 million, or 1.5 of its shares for each Morrison share. The hostile offer is valued at C$652 million.

Morrison on Wednesday delivered sharply higher results for 1996, posting a 108-percent jump in earnings per share to C$0.54 and an 18-percent increase in cash flow per share to C$1.47. Oil and gas reserves grew 39 percent to 88.5 million barrels of oil equivalent.

Stollery said momentum gained following a series of asset sales last year and the reduction of net debt to C$10 million by the end of this month would allow Morrison to post extremely strong first-quarter financial results as well.

"Notwithstanding having a great 1996, our profits in the first quarter of 1997 will be phenomenal because before we produce one drop of oil or one (thousand cubic feet) of gas, we're going to be booking a C$40 million gain on our royalty trust," he said.
The gain is expected to come as a result of Morrison's C$180 million sale of assets to a new oil and gas asset trust.

Stollery said shareholders should pay strong attention to the company's reported finding and development costs, which came in for 1996 at C$3.88 per BOE of proven reserves and C$2.13 per BOE of proven plus probable reserves.
"Those numbers are pretty hard to beat and are lower than Canadian 88's so-called representative numbers," he said.
Canadian 88 chief executive Greg Noval said last week that one reason for Morrison's recent disappointing stock market performamce was its record of high finding and development costs.

Stollery, who market watchers have predicted would fight Canadian 88's advance aggressively, said he was unable to suggest what the 1996 results meant in terms of Morrison's value until the company's financial advisers presented their findings to its board of directors, likely Friday or Monday.
Morrison shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange closed on Wednesday up 0.05 to 10.30. Canadian 88 was unchanged at 6.60. Morrison released its results following the close of trading.
